verdicts.strongest_argument: This is the captured wire copy, and the hunter names it as such: five different publishers, every one of them indexed in an admissible pre-print sweep. snapshots/20260901T153017Z.json alone carries 'Datadog Q2 2026: Revenue Up 36% and Guidance Raised, but the Stock Fell 17%' (line 169), 'Snowflake (SNOW) Sees Increased Bearish Options Activity Ahead of Earnings' (gurufocus, line 131-136), 'Snowflake Is Up Nearly 50% in 2026 - What Are Short Sellers Betting Against?' (Yahoo, line 120-125), the tipranks insider-sale piece (line 37) and the Cantor $405 target piece (line 147). Every component of the 'defensive positioning' cluster is a headline in one sweep, one session before the print. And the claim that 'every preview document in this capture frames the question as whether Snowflake beats. None of them frames it as whether beating is sufficient' is directly falsified twice by the same corpus: snapshots/20260901T153017Z.json line 41 indexes 'Snowflake options indicate 12% move on Sept 2 earnings' (investing.com), and snapshots/20260902T151912Z.json line 29 indexes 'Snowflake Q2 Preview: Stock Moved An Average Of 12.8% Last Seven Earnings Reports, Experts Says Buckle Up' (Benzinga). A published 12% implied move IS the market saying a beat may not be sufficient - it is the priced distribution, stated in a headline, and it is the single most direct rebuttal available to a 'the bar is higher than people think' argument. The Datadog analogue is itself the most-discussed software print of the season and sits in the same sweep the hunter read. The executive sale is a Form 4, public by mandate and already written up by tipranks. On the other side, the corpus also publishes the bull regime datapoint the hunter concedes - 'Gartner: Software Spend Now $1.44 Trillion in 2026, Revised Back Up to 15.1%' in snapshots/20260902T151912Z.json - so both halves of the debate are in the captured coverage. What is left is a stitched narrative over five published articles, which is analysis, not information. I withhold seven points only because the 12% implied-move article's body failed to fetch, so I have the headline number but not its construction.

prior_publication.what_it_says: Headline states Datadog grew revenue 36% and raised guidance and the stock still fell 17% - the finding's governing precedent, published as a headline in the sweep one session before the print.

Published pre-print that the options market implied a 12% move on the September 2 earnings - i.e. the priced distribution for this print was public, which is precisely the 'is a beat sufficient' question the finding says nobody asked.
A preview framing the print around a 12.8% average historical move and telling readers to 'buckle up' - preview copy that is explicitly about variance rather than about whether the company beats.
Publishes the increased bearish options activity ahead of earnings that the finding presents as unaggregated positioning evidence.
Publishes the short-seller thesis after the near-50% year - the third leg of the positioning cluster, in the same sweep.
The bull-side regime datapoint (software spend revised up to 15.1% growth) is published in the same capture, so the corpus carries both sides.

verdicts.baseline_evidence: The sealed baseline has no options fields, but the corpus supplies what they would have said: a pre-print headline putting the implied move at 12%, against a seven-event realised median of 13.43%. That is a market pricing a very wide distribution, which is the opposite of complacency. Run-up into the print is mildly negative (-3.02% 5d, -3.47% 20d) on 4.32m average shares, so the stock was already easing off its high before the print rather than melting up into it - the finding's 'exactly the position from which a good print gets sold' setup is a description of a price level, not of unpriced information. Six of seven prior prints were up, which the hunter acknowledges arguing against.
verdicts.what_would_change_it: Evidence that the published 12% implied move materially understated the distribution - for instance a dated skew or put-volume figure showing downside was cheap - which is exactly the datum no retrospective corpus can supply.
verdicts.note: The finding is honest that this is one argument from five publishers; my number reflects that all five are in the capture, not that the synthesis is worthless.

interactions: none across companies. Internally, the finding's bear cluster and its own conceded bull cluster (Gartner 15.1%, Atlassian/Twilio/Cloudflare) are both published in the same two sweeps, so the corpus records a contested debate rather than a blind spot.
corpus_limits: Several decisive SNOW items are index rows with 'fetch failed: HTTPError; no snippet in plan' - including the investing.com 12%-implied-move piece, the Benzinga preview and the tipranks insider piece - so I have their headlines and dates but not their bodies, and I have relied only on what the headline itself asserts. No options chain is recoverable retrospectively, so I cannot independently verify the 12% figure or read skew. I used snapshot 20260902T151912Z, whose sweep ran at 15:19Z on the event day: that is pre-print for an amc name sealed at the after-close 8-K, and I checked that the items I cite are previews rather than results copy, but a reader should discount them if they prefer a stricter cutoff. No document I used carried a non-empty tripwire_tells field.
